Cop a squat
KOP uh SKWOT
phrase (Silent Generation slang)
American slang for "sit down," recorded by the mid-20th century. Cop is old cant for to take or catch (whence cop, the policeman who catches), and squat, from Old French esquatir (to press down), is to crouch; so to cop a squat is to take a seat. It was a breezy invitation among servicemen, students and soda-fountain regulars.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

"Cop a squat" was how a friend said "sit down" in 1952 — at the soda fountain, in the barracks, around the kitchen table. It is a friendly phrase, an invitation to stay a while. Scripture is full of sitting, and much of it is holy. The peace God promised His people was a picture of sitting: "they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid" (Mic 4:4). Mary of Bethany chose the best seat in the house — at the Lord’s feet, where she "heard his word" (Luk 10:39). Where we sit also shows our hearts. The Lord told guests at a feast to "go and sit down in the lowest room" (Luk 14:10) rather than grab the best chair. And the greatest sitting of all is Christ’s. Having finished His work on the cross, He sat down at the right hand of the Father, as David foretold: "Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool" (Psa 110:1). Because He sits, His people may rest: "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest" (Mat 11:28). Grandchildren, when Grandpa tells you to cop a squat, he is offering you a place at his table. The Lord offers a better one, and it is never full.

Webster 1828 Definition

Silent Generation slang (mid-century American) for "sit down" — a friendly invitation that recalls the rest God promised: they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree (Mic 4:4).

expand to see more

COP A SQUAT, phrase (Silent Generation slang, 1950s; barracks, campus and soda-fountain talk) Sit down; take a seat. "Cop a squat and tell me how the game went."

Webster (1828) — SQUAT, verb intransitive 1. To sit down upon the hams or heels; as a human being. 2. To sit close to the ground; to cower; as an animal.

Decode for families: have a seat; the Lord says take the lowest room, and come to Him for rest.

Key Scripture

Mic 4:4 — "But they shall sit every man under his vine and under his fig tree; and none shall make them afraid: for the mouth of the LORD of hosts hath spoken it."

Luk 10:39 — "And she had a sister called Mary, which also sat at Jesus' feet, and heard his word."

Luk 14:10 — "But when thou art bidden, go and sit down in the lowest room; that when he that bade thee cometh, he may say unto thee, Friend, go up higher: then shalt thou have worship in the presence of them that sit at meat with thee."

Psa 110:1 — "A Psalm of David. The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool."

Mat 11:28 — "Come unto me, all ye that labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest."

Modern Corruption

A harmless and friendly phrase; the only thing to watch is the old habit of grabbing the best seat, which Jesus corrected.

expand to see more

There is nothing to correct in cop a squat. It is hospitality in slang — pull up a chair, you are welcome here — and hospitality is a Christian virtue.

The only lesson hiding in it is about where we sit. Jesus watched guests pick the chief seats and told them to take the lowest place instead. A child who learns to offer the good chair to Grandma has learned the parable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old cant cop (to take, catch) + Old French esquatir → squat (crouch) → mid-century cop a squat (take a seat).
